turns.t: Hello, doctor. It's my nose again. I thought the operation would sort it, but it's blocked again. Is it always going to be like this?
Let's have a proper look. When was the operation? ~
Eight months ago. The septum, and the turbinates. And it was lovely for about three months. Then it started creeping back.
Which side is blocked?
The left, mainly, and sometimes the right. Worse at night.
Anything else, discharge, loss of smell, pain in your face? ~
Clear drip, sometimes. No pain. My smell's okay. ~
What are you using for it?
The steroid spray, fluticasone, two sprays each side once a day, though I confess I don't use it every day.
Thanks for being honest. What else is in your medical history?
Hay fever, and asthma.
Do you smoke?
I vape. Not smoke.
Let me check you. Pulse and oxygen. ~
Okay. ~
Pulse 72, oxygen 99 percent, temperature 36.6.
All good? ~
All good. Now I'll look up your nose with the light. Tilt your head back.
Is it bad? ~
Your nasal lining is pink and swollen on both sides, particularly the left, and the septum looks straight, which is good. There's no pus and no polyps.
So what's wrong, then? ~
The swelling of the lining is what's blocking it, probably from your hay fever and the lining reacting, but I can't rule out some scarring inside from the surgery, which we can't see from here.
Scarring? ~
Adhesions, occasionally. It's possible, though not likely. ~
What do I do? ~
Use the fluticasone spray every day, even when you feel clear, for at least six weeks, because it only works when it's regular.
I'll set a reminder. ~
Add a salt-water rinse in the evenings, to clear the crusts and soothe the lining.
Do I make it myself? ~
You can buy sachets at the pharmacy. ~
Right. And if it doesn't help? ~
If you're still blocked after six weeks of regular use, come back and I'll refer you back to the ENT surgeon, who can look inside with a camera.
I understand. Thank you. ~
